title: Area VIII review: Postflight Procedures
intro: These questions mix the knowledge, risk and skills of Area VIII's one Task, checking instruments and equipment: writing up what went wrong in flight, the postflight inspection and servicing, and the records that keep the next IFR flight legal.

questions.q: Use the figure. In IMC the suction gauge drops to zero and you finish the flight partial panel. In an airplane with the system shown, which instruments do you list in the write-up as driven by the failed pump?
options: Attitude and heading indicators only; turn indicators are always electric
Attitude indicator only; the others have their own pumps
Attitude indicator, heading indicator and airspeed indicator
Attitude, heading and turn-and-slip indicators
questions.why: In this system the vane-type pump pulls air through the heading indicator, attitude indicator and turn-and-slip indicator [[23:113|IFH 5-18, Figure 5-28]]. A needle valve in the turn-and-slip line lowers its suction, since it needs only about 2 "Hg [[23:113|IFH 5-18, Figure 5-28]] [[23:112|IFH 5-17]]. Many airplanes use electric rate indicators instead, so know your own airplane's system [[23:112|IFH 5-17]]. The airspeed indicator is not on the vacuum lines in the figure.

questions.q: During cruise you tune both VOR receivers to the same station. VOR 1 shows 357° and VOR 2 shows 003°. On the ramp, what is the result of this dual VOR check?
options: A 6° split: it passes, since 6° is allowed in flight
A 6° split: it fails, so log it and write up the VORs
A 354° split: a dual check can't be done across north
A 3° error on each: it passes, since each is within 4°
questions.why: From 357° to 360° is 3°, and on to 003° is 3° more: 6° apart. A dual check allows at most 4° between the two bearings [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(c)]]. The 6° limit is for airborne checkpoints, not dual checks [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(b)(3)]], and a dual check gives no true reference to split the error. Enter the date, place and bearing error and sign [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(d)]].

questions.q: After a firm landing you find the ELT has been transmitting for about 25 minutes. The ELT record shows it also ran 40 minutes during an earlier false alarm. What goes in your write-up?
options: Nothing; ELT use only counts after a real accident
Reset it; the battery rule applies only past 50% of its life
The ELT battery must be replaced: more than 1 hour of total use
The ELT must be inspected again within 12 calendar months
questions.why: 25 + 40 = 65 minutes, more than 1 cumulative hour. ELT batteries must be replaced (or recharged, if rechargeable) when the transmitter has been in use for more than 1 cumulative hour, or when 50% of their useful life has expired [[1:239|PHAK 9-9]]. Either condition is enough. The 12-calendar-month ELT inspection is a separate, routine interval [[1:239|PHAK 9-9]].

questions.q: After an IFR flight in which the altimeter and VSI froze, you find a static port blocked by an insect nest. A mechanic disconnects a static line behind the panel to blow it clear, reconnects it and signs it off. Before your IFR flight in controlled airspace tomorrow, what else is needed?
options: Only the 43.9 entry; clearing a blockage isn't a tested item
A static system test and inspection under 91.411 first
Nothing more, as long as the alternate static valve is closed
Just a ramp check that the altimeter is within 75 ft
questions.why: After any opening and closing of the static system, other than use of the drains and alternate static valves, the system must be tested and inspected before IFR in controlled airspace [[60:524|14 CFR 91.411(a)(2)]]. The 75 ft altimeter check is a preflight accuracy check, not this test [[23:132|IFH 5-37]].

questions.q: The last altimeter, static system and encoder test was signed off on November 12, 2024. Reviewing the records after today's flight, what is the last day you may fly IFR in controlled airspace without a new test?
options: November 11, 2026
November 12, 2026
November 30, 2026
December 31, 2026
questions.why: The test must be within the preceding 24 calendar months [[60:524|14 CFR 91.411(a)(1)]]. A calendar-month period runs from any day of a month to the last day of that month at the end of the period; the PHAK explains it for 12 calendar months [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]]. So a November 12, 2024 test is good through November 30, 2026.

questions.q: There is no MEL. Your airplane's DME is dead, and it isn't required by any list, rule or AD for your flights. Rather than deactivate it, the owner has the shop remove it. Besides the 43.9 entry and placarding the control, what may the removal also call for?
options: A new altimeter and transponder test before the next IFR flight
Updating the weight and balance and the equipment list
A special flight permit to fly the airplane after the removal
A letter of authorization from the FSDO to operate without the DME
questions.why: Removal must be recorded under 43.9 with the cockpit control placarded [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(3)(i)]]. AC 91-67A adds that the authorized person also adjusts the weight and balance information and equipment list if required, submits a Form 337 as appropriate, and approves the return to service [[58:24|AC 91-67A 4.2.1]]. No approval or LOA is needed to operate under 91.213(d) [[58:23|AC 91-67A 4.1.1]].

questions.q: On the postflight walkaround at dusk you find the position lights don't work. You're scheduled to fly the airplane IFR again tonight, and there is no MEL. May the lights be deferred under 91.213(d) for that flight?
options: No; IFR at night needs the night VFR items, including position lights
Yes, if they are deactivated, placarded and judged not to be a hazard for this flight
Yes, because position lights aren't on the 91.205(d) list of IFR instruments
Yes, but only if you first get a special flight permit from the FSDO for tonight
questions.why: IFR flight requires the 91.205(b) items and, for night flight, the 91.205(c) items [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)(1)]], which include approved position lights [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(c)(2)]]. An item required by 91.205 for the kind of flight can't be deferred [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)(iii)]]. A special flight permit is for flying the airplane to where repairs can be made [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]].

questions.q: After landing you fill out the GPS anomaly report for a position jump you saw. Which item does the AIM list, 'if applicable', that you would not give for a VOR problem?
options: Date and time the anomaly was seen
Heading and altitude at the time
Number of satellites being tracked
Actions you took to deal with it
questions.why: A NAVAID or GPS anomaly report should include date and time, location, heading and altitude, avionics in use, number of satellites being tracked if applicable, a description and duration, the effect, actions taken, and postflight pilot or maintenance actions [[33:87|AIM 1-1-13]] [[33:88|AIM 1-1-13]]. Only the satellite count is GPS-specific. GPS problems go on the GPS Anomaly Reporting Form after the flight [[33:88|AIM 1-1-13]].

questions.q: You own your airplane and hold a private pilot certificate. Your postflight write-up lists a dead nav/comm. It is a self-contained, front panel-mounted unit with a tray connector, designed to be readily removed and replaced, and an identical approved unit with its instructions is on hand. What may you do?
options: Swap it as preventive maintenance, log it, and do the operational check
Swap it and fly IFR right away; a slide-in unit needs no operational check at all
Swap it, but only a mechanic may approve the airplane for return to service afterward
Nothing; any avionics work, even a slide-in swap, is for a mechanic or repair station
questions.why: Removing and replacing self-contained, front panel-mounted nav/comm units with tray-mounted connectors is preventive maintenance when the approved unit is designed to be readily and repeatedly removed and replaced and instructions are provided. It excludes autopilots, transponders and DME, and an operational check under part 91 is needed before use [[60:143|14 CFR Part 43, App. A(c)(31)]]. You may do preventive maintenance on an airplane you own [[60:130|14 CFR 43.3(g)]] and approve it for return to service [[60:132|14 CFR 43.7(f)]]. Your entry: work, date, name, signature, certificate number and type [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]]. For VOR use under IFR, that check includes 91.171 [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(a)]].

questions.q: The club airplane has two items legally deferred under 91.213(d): the autopilot and the landing light. You plan a single-pilot IFR flight tonight in rain, after a long day. What is the best way to think about it?
options: Legal isn't the end: weigh both items together with night, weather and workload
Go; the not-a-hazard finding for each item already covers this flight
Cancel; 91.213(d) allows only one deferred item at a time
Go, as long as the next required inspection isn't due yet
questions.why: Before flying with items inoperative under 91.213(d), weigh the effects of multiple items together, adverse weather, night, the airports, workload and crew fatigue [[58:25|AC 91-67A 4.4]]. A landing light isn't required for part 91 flights not for hire, but losing it still makes night flight more hazardous [[30:25|RMH 3-7]]. Give due consideration to an inoperative item's effect, particularly if other items are inoperative [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]].

questions.q: At the end of your flight, the records show the altimeter, static system and encoder test entry: 'tested to 12,000 ft.' Tomorrow you are filed IFR at 10,000 ft, and ATC may offer 14,000 ft to get above ice. Which is right?
options: You may take 14,000 ft, since the test is within 24 calendar months
The limit is only for the encoder, so take 14,000 ft with altitude reporting off
You may take 14,000 ft if you tell ATC about the test limit
You may not fly IFR in controlled airspace above 12,000 ft
questions.why: No one may operate under IFR in controlled airspace above the maximum altitude to which all altimeters and the automatic altitude reporting system were tested [[60:525|14 CFR 91.411(d)]]. Being within 24 calendar months doesn't remove that limit [[60:524|14 CFR 91.411(a)(1)]], and the rule covers the altimeters too, not just the encoder.

questions.q: IFR in controlled airspace, ATC tells you that you are 2 NM off your assigned route, but your GPS shows you on course with no flag or alert. You are near a large maintenance base. What should you do now and after landing?
options: Trust the GPS, because RAIM would have flagged any real position error to you by now
Change to another nav source, tell ATC, and file a GPS anomaly report later
Stay on the GPS and write it up only if the same thing happens to you a second time
Reset the GPS now, then tell only the maintenance shop about it after you land
questions.why: Faulty GPS re-radiators used for maintenance can cause unflagged, wrong position output; RAIM is only partly effective against this, and ATC may be the only way to detect it [[33:87|AIM 1-1-13]]. Change to another source and request amended clearances as needed [[33:87|AIM 1-1-13]]. Report the malfunction to ATC as soon as practical [[60:483|14 CFR 91.187(a)]], then use the GPS Anomaly Reporting Form after the flight [[33:88|AIM 1-1-13]].

questions.q: En route you tune a VOR and hear T-E-S-T in Morse code instead of its identifier, though the CDI looks normal. Other VORs identify normally on the same receiver. What do you do?
options: Write up the VOR receiver, since its ident audio is faulty on that station
Report it to ATC under 91.187 as a malfunction of your own nav equipment
Use it, since T-E-S-T means the station just passed its flight check and is reliable
Don't use it; the station is under maintenance, not your radio
questions.why: During maintenance, VHF ranges may radiate a T-E-S-T code. Removing the normal identification warns that the facility is off the air for tune-up or repair and may be unreliable even if signals are received [[33:87|AIM 1-1-11]]. Your receiver works on other stations, so it is not an airplane discrepancy.

questions.q: On your postflight write-up you note an aileron that binds. The shop replaces an aileron cable and signs it off, but says the work may have changed how the airplane flies and ground tests can't show otherwise. You want to take a friend on the next flight. What does 91.407 require first?
options: Nothing more; passengers may ride once the 43.9 entry is signed and approved
A pilot with at least a private certificate flies it, checks it and logs it
Only the mechanic who did the work may fly the check flight and log it afterward
The first flight after the repair needs a special flight permit from the FSDO
questions.why: No one other than crewmembers may be carried after maintenance that may have appreciably changed flight characteristics until a pilot with at least a private certificate flies the airplane, makes an operational check and logs the flight in the aircraft records [[60:521|14 CFR 91.407(b)]]. The flight can be skipped only if ground tests or inspection show conclusively that nothing changed [[60:521|14 CFR 91.407(c)]].

questions.q: You land after an IFR trip, and the airplane will sit in humid weather for two weeks with nothing booked. What is the best fuel servicing?
options: Fill the tanks to help prevent water condensation
Leave the tanks low to take weight off the tires
Drain the tanks down to the unusable fuel
Leave them as they are and fuel on the day of the next flight
questions.why: Add fuel based on the airplane's next use. If it will be inactive, filling the tanks is good practice to prevent water condensation inside them [[24:60|AFH 2-23]].

questions.q: Level at your assigned 7,000 ft with the current altimeter setting, ATC says: 'Stop altitude squawk, altitude differs by 400 feet.' After landing, the altimeter reads within 20 ft of field elevation with the current setting. What do you write up?
options: Nothing; the altimeter checks good, so the readout was ATC's error
The altimeter, since a wrong setting changes the altitude sent to ATC
The VSI, since a lagging VSI makes the readout wrong
The altitude reporting system, with the 400 ft difference ATC gave
questions.why: 'Stop altitude squawk, altitude differs' may mean the transmitted altitude is wrong or the altimeter setting is wrong. A wrong altimeter setting has no effect on the transmitted altitude; encoders are preset to standard pressure [[33:223|AIM 4-1-20]]. Your setting was current and the altimeter checks within 75 ft [[23:132|IFH 5-37]], which points to the altitude reporting system, part of the 24-month test [[60:524|14 CFR 91.411(a)(1)]].

questions.q: Flying IFR at night, your anticollision light fails en route. You land at your planned fuel stop, which has a maintenance shop open tonight. May you fly the second leg as planned?
options: Yes; an in-flight failure may be carried to your final destination
Yes, after you placard it INOP and note it in the record
No; you had to land at the nearest airport right away
No; you may continue only to a stop where it can be repaired
questions.why: Night flight requires an anticollision light system. If any light of it fails, operations may continue to a stop where repairs or replacement can be made [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(c)(3)]], and IFR at night includes the night VFR items [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)(1)]]. Your fuel stop is such a place. A placard alone can't defer an item 91.205 requires [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)(iii)]].

questions.q: Which postflight squawk gives the mechanic the most to work with?
options: Nav 2 CDI swung 10° with flag flickers, 1430Z, 5,000 ft, 20 NM E of XYZ, 3 min; Nav 1 normal
Nav 2 is junk again, same as last week and the week before; please replace the whole unit now
Nav 2 seemed off a few times in flight today but checked fine on the ground; please look at it
Possible bad VOR station near XYZ today; Nav 2 might be okay, please check it when you have time
questions.why: Erratic course indications and intermittent flags are exactly what should be reported [[33:87|AIM 1-1-13]]. A useful report gives time, location, altitude, the avionics in use, what happened and how long it lasted [[33:87|AIM 1-1-13]] [[33:88|AIM 1-1-13]]. Write it in the discrepancy record [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]]. Comparing Nav 1 on the same station shows it is the receiver, not the VOR.

questions.q: Gusty winds are forecast tonight, and the ramp tie-downs at this airport are chains. How should you secure the airplane?
options: Pull the chains taut so the airplane can't move at all
Skip the control locks, since the chains hold it in place
Leave slight slack so the airplane can move a little
Park tail to the wind so the chains carry less of the load
questions.why: Chains are not flexible, so they should not be made taut. Allowing the airplane some movement prevents airframe structural damage. Park headed into the wind when possible, secure the flight controls and put on the locks [[24:60|AFH 2-23]].

questions.q: After the shop repairs VOR 1, a radio repair station radiates a test signal and you do the VOR check. What must be in the aircraft log or other record?
options: Only your entry: date, place, bearing error and signature
Only the repair station's 43.9 entry; no pilot entry is needed
Your entry plus the repair station's entry of the bearing sent and date
Your entry plus an FSDO approval of the repair station's signal
questions.why: The person doing the check enters the date, place and bearing error and signs. When a repair station test signal is used, the repair station also enters the bearing it transmitted and the date [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(d)]]. Repair stations don't radiate the signal continuously, so verify which test radial is sent and whether you should get TO or FROM [[33:71|AIM 1-1-4]].
